label: text
text: Interesting details about London's annual meat bill, which, as shown by supplies to the Central Markets, reached a value £36,500,000 last year, are contained in the report for 1924 of the clerk and superintendent of the Smithfield Markets, Mr. H. G. W. Millman. Last year was a record for the markets, the total supplies (including poultry and provisions) amounting to 480,520 tons, which exceeded anything hitherto reached in the previous fifty-six years' history of the market. It is estimated that the live stock killed to furnish this food consisted of:

label: text
text: The total value of all commodities of £36,500,000 was in excess of the figure for the previous year by £1,500,000; this being attributed to the increase in supplies and the wholesale values of all classes of produce, except fresh-killed mutton and pork. One fact which emerges is that London's taste for mutton is decreasing at the expense of beef. Of the total supplies beef formed 55.2 per cent, mutton 27.8, and pork and bacon 10.5. In 1913 the ratio of mutton to beef was 3.9 per cent. higher.

label: text
text: How dependent the people of London, say 8,000,000 consumers, are upon the Central Markets for their meat was shown by the quantity distributed through the markets during the year—a quantity sufficient to provide each week a mixed-ration of beef, mutton, and pork of 38.7oz per head, viz., beef 22.9 oz, mutton 11.5oz, and pork 4.3oz; and how not only the public but meat traders rely upon overseas sources of supply, Colonial and foreign, was further shown by the fact that of the 38.7oz, the quantity of British-bred meats marketed was just sufficient to form 7.5oz per head, viz., beef 3.9 oz, mutton 2oz, and pork 1.6oz weekly. The position the market holds as the principal medium for the sale and distribution of the world's surplus meat supplies is shown by the following table of imports of beef and mutton into the United Kingdom in 1924 and the proportion handled at the market:

label: text
text: The value of the weekly list of retail prices, the issue of which was commenced last November, is commented upon. The list (states the superintendent) forms a price indicator, not only for London, but other parts of the country. It only embraces best quality meats—ewe mutton is not included—and if the people pay more, then they either lack the shopping or marketing sense, are indifferent, or require extra services which justify the retailer charging higher prices. Sections of the retail trade, who were critical, now help in a task which is generally conceded to be in the interests of all sections of the public from producer to consumer. The issue of the retail list should continue, for it affords the public information, and any appreciable fall in wholesale values, or rise, as the case may be, can be adjusted weekly in favour of or against the bearer of all charges—the consumer.

label: text
text: The average of the wholesale prices of Scotch sides of beef during 1924 was about 19.2 per cent above the average prices of other classes of fresh killed beef. Scotch and English mutton prices were lower than the year before, with the advantage in favour of the former, and realised 13.4 per cent higher values than other fresh mutton supplies—mostly Dutch, 72.3 per cent more than New Zealand mutton, and 100 per cent more than mutton from Australia and Argentina. Scotch and English lamb prices for 1924 were somewhat in favour of the home country. Chilled and frozen meat supplies from all sources totalled 317,994 tons. Of the total imports—900,808 tons—of beef, mutton, and lamb into the United Kingdom during the year 36.3 per cent. passed through the market for distribution, this being an increase of 1.2 per cent on 1923.

label: text
text: The earlier underwriting accounts of the year gave, it seems, a pretty good index of the state of affairs in marine insurance. The others are merely following on the same track. Of those published in the last week or two the London Assurance, it is true, transfers to profit an amount of £64,000, of which under £40,000 was earned in interest on funds. But that leaves in reserve only £1,000,000, against premiums last year totalling £1,122,000. The premium income of the London Assurance is particularly high, since before the war the annual premiums amounted only to around £400,000.

label: text
text: None of the other companies is so ambitious either as regards premiums or transfers to profit. The Alliance Assurance have put their interest receipts of £45,000 to profit, and on a premium income last year of £510,000 find their reserve a little less than at the end of 1923 at £1,008,000. The Royal Exchange Assurance are keeping their interest receipts in the underwriting account, and even so, on an increased premium income of £635,500, have only managed to increase their reserve by £40,000. It now stands at £792,000. The Phoenix Assurance is another company writing over £1,000,000 in premiums. The account is remarkable for the depletion of the reserve by over £400,000, notwithstanding that the first-year claims settlements for 1924 are rather lower than the average. The claims settled for previous years, totalling nearly £900,000, are very high, and, it would seem, another such year would seriously disturb the account.

label: text
text: It is interesting to learn that Mr. Elmsille, H.M. Trade Commissioner in New Zealand, considers that the Lancashire cotton trade is doing as well as ever it did so far as New Zealand is concerned, and, in fact, is showing gradual signs of development. He avers that the enthusiasm for British goods is such that purchasers will give up to 20 per cent more in order to obtain British-made in preference to foreign products. America and Japan, it is true, are doing their utmost to exploit the market, but Mr. Elmsille believes they are not making any headway, and in the matter of motor-cars and agricultural and dairying machinery in particular there is still considerable scope for the exporter in Great Britain.

label: text
text: Not only is the soap consumed in the United Kingdom lower in price and higher in quality than that of any other country, but as a natural result the United Kingdom enjoys a larger export trade in soap to neutral markets of the world that of the total exports of soap of any other three nations added together," said Lord Leverhulme at the annual meeting of Lever Brothers.

label: text
text: Speaking of the present high taxation of Great Britain, he said that against this inequality the British taxpayer gained the advantage of the high standard of exchange. British credit had been maintained, and of the two evils high taxation or low rate of exchange we had chosen wisely in preferring high taxation. But, all the same, he added, British trade and commerce were staggering under this heavy burden.

label: text
text: With Great Britain, the Philippines overseas trade for April, 1925, was valued at P2,902,877, of which P1,916,829 represented the value of exports. Trade with China went over the two-million peso mark, but the Philippine exports for last month amounted to only a little over P500,000. The same was true of the export trade with Japan, the products sent to that country amounting to over P800,000 which was less than the imports from the island empire. The total trade with Japan for April, 1925, was P2,145,775.

label: text
text: The United States as usual obtained the lion's share of the Philippine trade for the month under review, the import and export trade with that country amounting to P29,425,893, or more than half the total. Of this sum, P20,906,862 represented the value of Philippine products that went to the United States during that month and the rest, imports from that country into the Philippines.

The overseas trade of the Philippines for April, 1925, showed an increase of more than P5,000,000 over the trade for the corresponding month in 1924, the figures being P43,143,944 and P38,078,333, respectively, according to a complete compilation of trade accounts made public by the statistical division of the bureau of customs.
The balance of trade was in favour of the Philippines by more than P11,000,000, according to the report, the exports of the country for April, 1925, amounting to P27,197,764 as against P15,946,176 worth of imports during the same period.

label: text
text: Sir Charles Greenway, who has recently returned from Buenos Aires, is reported to have said that he was greatly impressed with the markable progress of that country, but was disappointed by the attitude adopted by the Argentine Government towards foreign capital engaged in the oil fields. The trouble is that some of the lands in the Comodoro Rivadavia field which the Anglo-Persian had acquired, and on which a producing well had been brought in have been included within the limits of the enlarged national oil reserve formed by the Argentine Government. The claims of the Anglo-Persian, which would appear to be strong, have been ignored. The Argentine Government has committed itself to a policy of intensive oil development by the State. The Budget for 1925 includes an appropriation for an increased drilling campaign the construction of further storage tanks, and the purchase of another tank steamship. On its oil operations in 1924 the Government claims to have made a surplus of three million pesos. This has probably counted against Sir Charles Greenway.
